title: Build a News Feed
summary: Design Murmur's home feed interview style: fan-out on read vs on write, the celebrity problem, a hybrid feed cache, ranking and pagination inside a 200 ms budget.

goals.text: Size a feed system from a few assumptions
Compare fan-out on read with fan-out on write
Solve the celebrity problem with a hybrid
Fit ranking and pagination into a 200 ms budget
Handle cold users, hot posts and deletes

steps.title: What a feed has to do
body: The prompt: “Design the home feed for a social app.” Murmur lets people post short updates and scroll a feed of posts from everyone they follow.

Functional: post, follow, read a ranked, infinitely scrolling feed. Non-functional is where it gets interesting: the feed must open in under 200 ms, new posts should reach followers within seconds, and we can accept a little staleness in exchange for speed.

card.title: Requirements
lines: **must**: home feed of people you follow
**must**: new posts show up within seconds
# a few seconds of staleness is fine

steps.title: The numbers that shape it
body: With 200 million daily users opening the feed 10 times a day, that's about 23,000 feed reads a second. Half of them post once a day: about 1,200 posts a second.

Reads outnumber writes 20 : 1, but every post has to reach ~200 followers. If we pre-compute feeds, that's ~230,000 small writes a second. Storing the latest 500 post ids per user costs about 4 KB each, roughly 800 GB in total: a Redis cluster can hold that.

card.title: Back of the envelope
lines: = 500 ids × 8 B per user → ~800 GB of feeds

steps.title: Two calls and a cursor
body: Posting is a POST returning the new id. Reading is GET /v1/feed, twenty items at a time.
Paging uses an opaque cursor, not a page number. With offsets, every new post pushes older ones down, so “page 2” would repeat items the user just saw. A cursor says “continue after this item”.

card.title: The API
lines: # cursor, not page number: new posts
# would shift every offset and repeat items

steps.title: First sketch: build the feed on read
body: The simplest design: a Post service writes posts, and a Feed service builds each feed when it's opened. It asks the follow graph “who does this reader follow?”, fetches the newest posts from each, merges and sorts.
This is fan-out on read. Posting is cheap and new posts are visible instantly. But one feed open costs about 200 lookups.
changes: + Load balancer, Post and Feed services

steps.title: Deep dive: reads explode
body: At the evening peak, 70,000 feed opens a second × 200 lookups is 14 million post reads a second, almost all of them repeating work done seconds earlier for another reader.
The Posts DB runs hot, merging 200 timelines takes time, and feeds take well over a second to open. We spend the expensive work at the worst moment: while a person is waiting.

callout.text: Fan-out on read makes the common operation (reading) pay for the rare one (posting).

changes: ~ Feed service merges 200 timelines per request

steps.title: Fan-out on write
body: Flip it. When Kai posts, the Post service emits a PostCreated event. Fan-out workers look up Kai's followers and prepend the post id to each follower's list in a feed cache.
Opening a feed is now one list read plus fetching 20 posts by id. The expensive work happens in the background, about two seconds after posting, while nobody is waiting.

callout.text: Lists are capped at 500 ids: nobody scrolls further, and the cap keeps memory predictable.

steps.title: Deep dive: the celebrity problem
body: Then Nova, a singer with 50 million followers, posts. One post becomes 50 million cache writes. At 25,000 writes a second for her share of the fleet, the last fans see it after about half an hour, and everyone else's posts queue behind hers.
Most of those writes are wasted, too: many of her followers won't open the app today.

steps.title: Push for most, pull for a few
body: Use both models. Accounts with more than about 100,000 followers skip fan-out. At read time, the Feed service takes the reader's pre-built list and merges in recent posts from the handful of celebrities they follow, which stay hot in cache because millions read them.
Also skip pushing to followers who haven't opened the app in 30 days. Their feed is rebuilt on return.

callout.text: Pick the model per account, not per system: push is cheap for small audiences; pull is cheap for huge ones.

changes: ~ Post service skips fan-out for big accounts
~ Feed service merges list + celebrity posts

steps.title: Rank inside the budget
body: Pure newest-first isn't what people want. The feed list gives ~500 candidates; a Ranker scores each on signals like recency, how often you interact with the author, and early engagement, then returns the top 20.
Everything must fit the 200 ms budget, so lay it out explicitly. Ranking gets the biggest slice; hydration is a single multi-get; and some headroom is left for the slow tail.

steps.title: Pages, cold users, hot posts
body: Pagination: the cursor holds the (score, post_id) of the last item, read against a short-lived snapshot of the ranked list, so page 2 never repeats page 1.

Lia returns after three months. No list exists for her, so her first feed is rebuilt the slow way, by pulling from the people she follows, then cached. A viral post becomes a hot key: replicate it across cache nodes. Deleted posts are filtered out when hydrating.
changes: ~ Feed rebuilt from the follow graph

card.title: Pages and edge cases
lines: = session snapshot: page 2 never repeats page 1
! inactive 30+ days → no pushes, rebuild on return
! viral post → hot key: replicate it in the post cache
! deleted post → filtered out at hydrate time

steps.title: Murmur's feed
body:
• Fan-out on read: cheap posts, expensive reads. Fine at small scale.
  • Fan-out on write: pre-built feeds in a cache; reads become one list fetch.
  • Celebrities break push: go hybrid, pull big accounts at read time.
  • Skip inactive users; rebuild their feed on return.
  • Rank a few hundred candidates within an explicit latency budget.
  • Cursor pagination over a snapshot avoids duplicates.
